topic: The spotlight effect: nobody's watching you as much as you think
title: Nobody's Watching You As Much As You Think
voiceover: Do you think everyone noticed that mistake? In 2000, psychologist Thomas Gilovich and colleagues published the first empirical evidence of the spotlight effect. Students wore an embarrassing Barry Manilow T-shirt into a room of other students. The wearers guessed that about 46 percent of the others would notice the shirt. In reality, only about 23 percent did. That means they overestimated by about double. Researchers call this the spotlight effect: we overestimate how much others notice us. They attribute it to egocentrism: you experience your own flaws so intensely that you assume others do too. Next time you feel watched, remember the shirt study: people notice you roughly half as much as you expect. Tomorrow: why does $9.99 feel so much cheaper than $10?

description: Do you think everyone noticed your slip-up? In a classic study, people wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about twice as many classmates would notice it as actually did. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Gilovich, T., Medvec, V. H., & Savitsky, K. (2000). The spotlight effect in social judgment: An egocentric bias in estimates of the salience of one's own actions and appearance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 78(2), 211-222.
accuracy_note: Percentages (46% predicted vs 23% observed) come from secondary summaries of the paper; the PDF could not be opened from this environment. The effect was shown with college students in a lab. Egocentrism is the authors' proposed explanation.
